text: If you could change the ending of High Tension, how would you do it? The ending of High Tension was... controversial, to say the least, as many of you may know. Despite ample foreshadowing (so much foreshadowing, in fact, that they may as well have revealed it well before the climax), the twist is still completely out of left field and creates a number of plot holes, most glaringly, the fact that the killer was spotted having sex with a severed head in his truck just outside the cornfield at the start. To be perfectly honest, I would prefer a standard — albeit gory — slasher over the mess that ending caused. I don't blame Aja for the ending, really, because he was forced into it by the studio, who wanted a twist ending. He just went with probably the most lazy, overused ending he could. But I have my own, partially fleshed-out idea for an ending. The climax would begin at the same point, where Marie follows the killer's truck after nearly losing him. Except she actually came prepared and loaded the gun beforehand. This would fit in with her character better, since she used quick thinking earlier to rearrange the bedroom so it would look like nobody's staying there. When the killer spots her, she fires a few rounds, managing to hit his tires and forcing him off the dirt road. By pure slasher movie logic, he survives and gets out of the truck, while Marie runs off to the woods to look for Alex and to finish off the killer (hey, this is the same movie where a guy gets decapitated by a bookshelf, okay? I'm allowed to use some artistic license), who ambushes her the same way as before. The fight that ensues is the exact same as in the original, minus Marie's guttural scream, which I'll be saving for... She searches the killer's body, takes his keys and unlocks the back of the truck, hoping to find Alex alive and well. Unfortunately, Alex is either bleeding heavily from blunt force trauma and dies shortly after Marie finds her, or is already dead, which leads to the aforementioned scream, followed by Marie whispering her mantra, "I won't let anyone come between us anymore" over and over again. Cut back to the hospital, end movie. Additionally, I would like to include a little more development towards Marie and Alex's relationship. It's made clear throughout that Marie is a barely closeted lesbian with strong, unreciprocated feelings for Alex, maybe even being protective of her to an unhealthy extent. It would make her mantra, plus all the unresolved sexual tension between the two make just as much sense — if not more — as it did in the original ending. The split personality imagery and foreshadowing would be toned down to be either red herrings, like having Marie question her sanity, or removed completely, and the killer would ultimately serve as being a sort of shadow to Marie, killing women and their families out of a perverted obsession and a need to covet the women for himself. What do you think?

text: Wes Craven's New Nightmare (1994) — 32 Years Later. New Nightmare came out 32 years ago today, so I figured I'd give it another watch as part of my Halloween marathon. Going back to my first viewing, I liked this one quite a bit, and it has always stood out to me from the rest of the Nightmare on Elm Street sequels. By this point in the series, Freddy had pretty much become a comedian who occasionally murdered people, so I love that Craven decided to bring back the creepy side of the character. The whole idea of Freddy haunting the actors and people behind the movies is a pretty clever way to do it, I think. Heather Langenkamp playing herself works really well, and I like how the movie blurs the line between what's real and what's part of the franchise. It's a little weird, a lot darker than the previous few movies, and actually manages to make Freddy feel threatening again. Not bad for the seventh entry in a series. It's not without its flaws, and I wouldn't put it above the original or Dream Warriors, but I think it's one of the better sequels. It's also funny looking back at how Craven was already messing around with meta-horror a couple of years before Scream. 4/5 ⭐️ – Clever premise, a genuinely creepy Freddy, and one of the franchise's strongest sequels. A few pacing issues keep it from being a five-star movie. Anyone else really like this one? Where would you rank it in the franchise?

text: Some of my favourite moments in Obsession (2026) Ok. I feel like I just want to rant about this film a bit so if you aren't interested just scroll away. Spoilers ahead also. The first thing I want to say is that ive watched it in theatres 5 times, and after seeing all of Curry Barker's horror short films I LOVEEEEEE his fucked up brain. seeing so many similar elements and ideas makes me so happy and I absolutely love how he creates the perfect spooky ambiance in moments that aren't even supposed to be scary. One of my most favourite theories is that Bear is stinky, and with every re-watch I notice more an more that proves this theory. From leaving the cat in his apartment, to not noticing that it was the cat in his sandwich, not flinching when he opens the door in the scene where Nikki pisses and shits everywhere. like he does notice it when the lights come on, but there is a period of at least 5 seconds where he comes in and hasn't turned on the lights, how did he not instantly throw up because of the smell?????? someone explain it because that doesnt make sense to me. And I also love how when Nikki first enters the apartment she takes a huge whiff and basically moans afterwards, and then in the kitchen she says it smells like him and his automatic response is, "does it smell bad?" like HE KNOWS he's smelly and that proves it! Another thing I love is the evolution of Nikki's jewelry to show her changing. she starts off super heavily accessorized and wearing silver, and then slowly she starts wearing less and less, then she makes th switch to gold when she wears the necklace with a B on it, and I LOVE when they are at the party, notably the scene when the most shit goes down in terms of her character progression, and she is literally wearing a SPIRAL NECKLACE????????? to represent her spiralling of course, but I thought that was so clever. I watched so many interviews with her stylist and she said that it was a purposeful choice and even down to the fact that Nikki almost exclusively wears shirts that expose her chest area to signify an increase in vulnerability and control shifting towards Bear. we love that. the attention to detail is exquisite. One thing I do have to say though is that im glad I watched this on opening night when there was still no buzz on social media about it. going in with no exposure to the more "meme-worthy" parts of the film, it genuinely shook me to my core. I was so captivated by the sound editing and the amazing cinematography, that I was actually scared outta my mind. but going back to watch it countless times, I notice that the audience started changing and it went from a group of horror freaks that were actually scared to then a group of teenagers who were laughing and joking and quoting all the TikTok scenes throughout the film. Im glad I got to see it at the time that I did, because I was able to appreciate the film for the absolute masterpiece that it is. thats all I guess, I would love to hear what anyone else has to say about this, any other fun theories, any thing you may have missed that you caught in a re-watch. text: A reflection of "Barbarian" A long time ago, I fell out of the habit of watching movies. Back when VHS tapes were still a thing, I loved going to the video rental store and picking out three or four horror movies to watch with my friends over the weekend. The Blob, Friday the 13th, Children of the Corn, Child's Play, Gremlins... I was completely obsessed. About two months ago, I decided to get back into it. Now, every night after work, I sit down and watch one or two movies. I have to say, that passion has come back stronger than ever. It's fascinating to see how much the horror genre has evolved. It has reinvented itself, becoming far more refined, better crafted, and filled with genuinely engaging stories. Barbarian is one of those movies that I absolutely loved discovering. It had me hooked from beginning to end. It's strange, unsettling, dark, and bizarre in just the right measure. I wouldn't say it genuinely scared me because, at my age, I don't really get frightened by movies anymore—I always know they're just movies. That's why I connect much more with the other emotions they evoke: the sense of unease, the unpredictability, the discomfort, the atmosphere, the cinematography, and the originality of a well-told story. Barbarian delivers all of that remarkably well. I've seen some people say the movie loses steam in its second half. Well, I couldn't disagree more. I loved the second half just as much as the first. An outstanding film that avoids the usual slasher, ghost, and demon clichés. Barbarian has definitely earned a special place in my heart. 10/10

text: Resident Evil Review (SPOILERS) Let me start off by saying that I have played Resident Evil since it first released in 1996 for the original PlayStation. I have played every main line game including the remakes. I am a huge Resident Evil fan and have been for the last 30 years. So, those are my credentials to give an opinion on this film. The movie is absolutely brilliant. I have been anticipating this film since it got announced and the minute I saw Zach Creger was directing, I had instant faith in whatever direction he was choosing to go and I was not disappointed one bit. Austin Abram’s does a fantastic job in the leading roll and plays the part so damn well. His line delivery is so spot on along with his reactions to what is going on around him. It truly makes you believe and feel he is a normal dude working his way through an absolute shit show. It’s worth watching just for his performance alone. The cinematography is beautiful. The shots, the camera angles, the choice in colors for each area and the set pieces are exactly what you would get in the game. The goal of this movie was not to re-do what’s already been done and it accomplishes exactly what it was meant to do. It takes you into the world and grabs you immediately and I could not feel more like I was witnessing the game. I’m still in awe of how well done the cinematography is and it sets the stage like no other Resident Evil film, anime or tv show has ever been able to capture. While I’m on the topic of the previous entries of Resident Evil in film, yes I have watched Paul WS Anderson’s shit show of seven movies, the Netflix show, and the animated films along with the bullshit Welcome to Raccoon City. Zach Creger has fully accomplished bringing a brand new story while honoring what Resident Evil games do so well and it’s transporting you into a world of monsters, terror, and comedic relief. I’m going to flat out it say it and this is where I find this to be a huge SPOILER for the vibe of this film. If you have not seen it, you may not want to read forward. This is a comedy and through and through and it’s one of the best Comedic Horror movies I’ve seen since 28 Years Later: The Bone Temple (that’s an entirely different discussion). I laughed a lot and so did the rest of the theater. Zach Creger’s comedic timing is out of this world and Austin Abram’s delivery of the lines are so well placed through out the film. I figured it would be funny at times based on what I’ve heard about it but I was not expecting to laugh as much as I did. This falls very much into the realm of Return of the Living Dead, Shaun of the Dead, and the Evil Dead. text: Finally watched The Substance - how did everyone feel about the ending? I almost always enjoy horror movies. I was really looking forward to this one - I had heard good things, and a modern take on body horror was a compelling idea to me. I find that a lot of big box office horror/thriller movies fumble the ending. In 2024, I felt that way about Longlegs and Late Night with the Devil. Both of those movies had me roped in for the first 2/3 or 3/4 but went in disappointing directions for the ending - in Late Night with the Devil's Case, the last ten minutes or so. I LOVED the first 98% of that movie, but the hokiness factor skyrocketed out of nowhere just before the finish line. Unfortunately, I felt the same about The Substance. I have plenty of positive things to say about the movie. The visuals and acting were top notch. The gruesome cinematography was so vivid that I had to look away a few times. The writing and character work were clever - the film managed to explain the process of the main "experience" with very minimal dialogue, which was refreshing. Some of the more introspective scenes, like the date prep scene, were just as incredible in that they expressed Elisabeth's internal conflict without hitting you over the head with it. The suspense, implicit characterization, and pacing were all excellent - I did not feel bored or like the movie was dragging AT ALL for the duration of the run time. I really appreciated the storytelling too. I feel like body horror is always at its best when it's a metaphor for something larger - in this case, the way society callously discards women when they're "past their prime" physically. But the clever way that the movie sets up its central metaphor is why I was so disappointed in the ending. I actually liked the idea of Elisasue and the climax at the New Year's show - that sort of catharsis worked after the buildup of suspense surrounding the show, and the idea of the younger version STILL not being "good enough" was a great theme to end on. The metaphor was there, 100%, but I audibly groaned when Elisabeth's disembodied face crawled over to die on top of the Hollywood star, especially combined with Sue repeating "Please give me a younger, better version of me!" into the mirror, out loud, only a few minutes before. It just felt so ON THE NOSE compared to the writing in the rest of the movie. Like they really spent two hours setting up a powerful conflict with broader metaphorical implications, only to be suddenly become so heavy handed in the ending. It doesn't make me dislike the film at all, and it thematically works just fine. I was just very impressed with the (relative) subtlety of the first two hours, which made the sudden switch to "We are telegraphing in the most direct and overt way possible exactly what you're supposed to take away from this movie" a very jarring note to end on for me. Curious to hear everyone else's thoughts

text: The Lighthouse (2019) Refuses to Explain Itself and I Love It. After watching *The Witch*, I thought I had already experienced the peak of Robert Eggers' atmosphere. Then I watched *The Lighthouse*, and somehow its atmosphere managed to haunt me in completely different ways. # The Plot I honestly struggle to place this film into a single genre, which feels fitting because the movie itself is such a mystery. If I had to choose, I'd simply call it a mystery. The claustrophobic setting, combined with the uncertainty and unease of being stranded on a remote island, works incredibly well. What I loved most is how little the film commits to any single explanation. Nothing is decisively proven true. Every interpretation feels possible. >!Normally, I'm not a fan of films that lean heavily on hallucinations or dream logic, but *The Lighthouse* somehow made it work for me. Even if the entire story were simply Howard's dying dream, I wouldn't mind, because the film never forces that conclusion.!< It remains ambiguous right until the end, leaving the viewer to decide what really happened. # The Cinematography I knew going in that it was black and white. What I didn't expect was the aspect ratio. It's practically a square. That single decision immediately transported me to another era. It didn't just feel like an old movie. It felt older than most old movies. I later read that Eggers chose the ratio partly to emphasize the film's claustrophobic nature, and it works brilliantly. The frame constantly feels restrictive, trapping the characters and the audience alike. Combined with the stark black-and-white photography, the harsh lighting, and the cramped framing, the result is one of the most visually distinctive horror films I've ever seen. # The Characters There are only two main characters. >!Or maybe only one, depending on how you interpret the story.!< Either way, both Willem Dafoe and Robert Pattinson absolutely nail their roles. The dynamic between the domineering older keeper and the increasingly submissive younger one creates constant tension. >!What I found especially fascinating is how the film weaves in mythological themes. The story can be read through Prometheus and Proteus, yet it never feels like a straightforward retelling. !<It takes familiar ideas and presents them in a way that feels completely original. # The Dialogues Oh, how I love the dialogues. I genuinely think some of these lines will stay with me for the rest of my life. The script is darkly funny, endlessly quotable, and unlike anything else I've heard in modern cinema. One moment it's poetic and theatrical, the next it's absurdly hilarious. My personal favorites have to be the curse speech and the fart one. >"I'm sick of your laughing, your snoring..." >"...and your goddamned farts. Your damned goddamned farts. Goddamn yer farts!" Bruh. I was absolutely dying during that scene. # Criticism This definitely won't be for everyone. If you need a straightforward plot with clear answers, *The Lighthouse* may frustrate you. It refuses to explain what is real, what is imagined, and what any of it finally means. The pacing can also test patience. A lot of the film is built around repeated routines: work, drinking, arguments, hallucinations, and power struggles. For some viewers, that may feel less like progression and more like being trapped in the same cycle. >!The symbolism is heavy too. The Prometheus and Proteus parallels are fascinating, but !<if you are not into mythological readings, parts of the film may feel deliberately obscure. The dialogue is brilliant, but the old-fashioned language and thick accents can make some lines hard to catch on a first watch. And if you are expecting traditional horror, this may disappoint you. There is dread, tension, and disturbing imagery, but not many conventional scares. It is more about isolation, guilt, fixation, and madness than simple fear. # Final Thoughts >!Personally, I lean toward the interpretation that the entire film may have been Howard's dying dream.!< But after reading other theories online, what fascinates me is that many of them make sense as well. That's probably what I admire most about *The Lighthouse*. It doesn't hand you answers. It gives you pieces and trusts you to assemble them yourself. It's a strange, haunting, funny, unsettling, and unforgettable experience.

text: Tumbbad (2018, India, Folk Horror) This movie is amazing. India is the second largest film industry on the planet, but they rarely make horror movies, and when they do it's usually comedy horror, and we're now seeing a renaissance of real Indian Horror propelled by the 2000s movie "13B" and by this movie. You arguably wouldn't have amazing movies like "Bramayugam" or "Bulbbul" without the success of Tumbbad. It has extremely beautiful cinematography and all on-location shootings, most of it in the actual village of Tumbbad. A passion project that took over 10 years to make. This is folk horror that breaks several of the rules of the genre, as it's much more personal. It's one of the best movies ever made about generational trauma; it explores it in such an in-depth way, all the ramifications of it, how it affects children, how it's passed on, and the intricate class and gender dynamics of it, all wrapped up in the subtext of a story about greed. It mixes ancient Hindu stories with Lovecraft mythos in a full hybridization of the two, giving it a truly eerie ambiance. An absolute must watch.
label: statement
